h: Gospels, gardens and a day ruled by the sea
p: Holy Island's most famous treasure isn't on the island at all. The Lindisfarne Gospels, a stunning illuminated manuscript, were created here in the early 700s, most likely in honour of St Cuthbert. Today they're kept at the British Library in London, but standing among the priory ruins you're right where that extraordinary work began.

Lindisfarne Castle, perched on its rocky crag, is looked after by the National Trust, and the little walled garden near it was designed by Gertrude Jekyll. Even if you don't go inside the castle, the walk out to it along the shore is lovely, with views back to the priory and village.

At low tide, the tiny islet of St Cuthbert's Isle, just off the priory, can be reached on foot, and it's where the saint sought solitude. Don't get caught out, though. The same applies to the Pilgrims' Way, the ancient route across the sands marked by tall poles. It's a special experience, but the tide comes in fast, so only attempt it with proper knowledge of the timings.

Allow at least half a day once you've crossed, more if you're walking the island's coast. In the busy season the village can get crowded in the middle of the day, so arriving earlier or staying later can feel calmer. Back on the mainland, Bamburgh Castle is a short drive south, while Berwick-upon-Tweed, with its walls and riverside walks, is just up the road to the north.
